t.7.61.1: Hearing those words spoken by the great-souled Śatrughna, he was seized with fierce anger and cried, "Stay! Stay!"
t.7.61.2: Grinding hand against hand and gnashing his teeth, Lavaṇa challenged the tiger of the Raghus again and again.
t.7.61.4: Śatrughna had not yet been born when the others were conquered by you. Therefore today, struck down by my arrows, go to the abode of Yama.
t.7.61.5: O wicked-souled one, today let the sages, too, the learned brahmins, behold you slain by me in battle, just as the gods beheld Rāvaṇa.
t.7.61.3: To Lavaṇa of terrible prowess, who was speaking those words, O slayer of the enemies of the gods, Śatrughna spoke this reply.
t.7.61.6: When you, O night-wanderer, have fallen today, consumed by my arrows, this city and the countryside as well will be secure.
t.7.61.7: Today an arrow released from my arm, its tip like the thunderbolt, shall pierce your heart, as a ray born of the sun enters a lotus.
t.7.61.8: Thus addressed, Lavaṇa, overcome with rage, hurled a mighty tree at Śatrughna's chest, but the hero cut it into a hundred pieces.
t.7.61.9: Seeing that his effort had proved fruitless, the mighty rākṣasa once again seized a great many trees and hurled them at Śatrughna.
t.7.61.10: And the radiant Śatrughna, too, cut down each of the many trees hurtling toward him, one by one, with three or four smooth-jointed arrows.
t.7.61.11: Then Śatrughna, endowed with valour, released a shower of arrows upon the rākṣasa's chest, yet the rākṣasa did not waver.
t.7.61.12: Then Lavaṇa, laughing, uprooted a tree as if in play and struck the hero on the head; his limbs going slack, he indeed fell into a swoon.
t.7.61.13: When that hero had fallen, a great cry of lamentation arose from the sages, the hosts of gods, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases as well.
t.7.61.14: Disregarding Śatrughna, thinking him slain and struck down upon the ground, the rākṣasa, though he had gained the opportunity, did not enter his own dwelling.
t.7.61.16: After a moment, having regained consciousness, Śatrughna, weapon in hand, stood once more at the rākṣasa's gate, honored by the sages.
t.7.61.15: Seeing him felled upon the ground, he did not even take up the trident again; then, knowing that he was slain, he gathered up those victuals.
t.7.61.17: Then he took up that supreme, divine and unfailing arrow, terrible, blazing with fiery energy and filling the ten directions.
t.7.61.18: An arrow with a thunderbolt for its head and the speed of the thunderbolt, as heavy as Meru and Mandara, curved at all its joints and never defeated in battles.
t.7.61.20: Seeing him blazing like the fire of Time when the end of the age has arrived, all beings fell into great terror.
t.7.61.19: That winged shaft with beautiful feathers, its body smeared with blood and sandal paste, dreadful to the lords of the Dānavas, to the lords of the mountains, and to the Asuras.
t.7.61.21: For the whole world, together with the Devas, Asuras and Gandharvas, with the sages and with the hosts of Apsarases, was distressed and approached the Grandfather.
t.7.61.22: And they said to the lord of the gods of gods, the boon-granting great-grandsire: "O god, is this the destruction of the worlds, or has the end of the yuga arrived?"
t.7.61.24: Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the grandsire of the worlds, the giver of fearlessness, explained to the gods the cause of their fear.
t.7.61.23: Such a thing has never been seen or heard of before, O Great-Grandsire: the gods bewildered by fear and the worlds facing destruction, O lord.
t.7.61.25: The arrow borne by Śatrughna for the slaying of Lavaṇa in battle, by whose splendour all of us, the best of the gods, were bewildered.
t.7.61.27: This mighty arrow was indeed created by that great-souled one for the sake of Kaiṭabha and Madhu, for the slaying of those two Daityas.
t.7.61.26: For this, O dear ones, is the eternal arrow, made of fiery splendor, that formerly belonged to the god, the maker of the worlds, the arrow through which terror came about.
t.7.61.28: Know this arrow, then, to be thus, made of the fiery energy of Viṣṇu; and this indeed is the former body of that great-souled Viṣṇu.
t.7.61.29: Come here, all of you, and behold Lavaṇa, the foremost of rākṣasas, being slain by the great-souled hero, the younger brother of Rāma!
t.7.61.30: Having heard that sweet speech of the God of gods, they came to the place where the two, Śatrughna and Lavaṇa, were fighting.
t.7.61.31: All beings beheld that divine-looking arrow held in Śatrughna's hand, like the fire risen up at the end of the age.
t.7.61.32: Seeing the sky covered by the gods, the delight of the Raghus roared like a lion again and again and looked once more at Lavaṇa.
t.7.61.33: Then, challenged by that great-souled Śatrughna, Lavaṇa, filled with rage, came forward for battle.
t.7.61.35: Having gone to the divine Rasātala, the arrow honored by the gods swiftly returned once more to the delight of the Ikṣvāku race.
t.7.61.34: Then he, the best of bowmen, drew that bow back to his ear and released a mighty arrow at the broad chest of Lavaṇa. Swiftly tearing open his chest, it entered Rasātala.
t.7.61.36: Pierced through by Śatrughna's arrow, that night-roaming Lavaṇa suddenly fell to the ground like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
t.7.61.37: And when the rākṣasa Lavaṇa had been slain, that great divine trident, while all beings looked on, returned into the power of Rudra.
t.7.61.38: Having destroyed the fear of these three worlds with the fall of a single arrow, the foremost hero of the Raghus, his bow and arrow upraised, shone forth like the thousand-rayed sun that has dispelled the darkness.
